description: Benchmark figures from OpenStax Introductory Statistics 2e, Chapter 2 (CC BY 4.0). True values come from the textbook's own tables and text; null where the book gives none. Reference descriptions are drafts. Every entry needs a human check (verified: false). expected_outcome: auto_approve = the agent should approve it; needs_review_ok = sending it to human review also counts as correct.

figures.caption: Figure 2.1 When you have large amounts of data, you will need to organize it in a way that makes sense. These ballots from an election are rolled together with similar ballots to keep them organized.

reference.alt_text: Rolled paper election ballots bundled together in a pile, with the chapter title Descriptive Statistics overlaid.

figures.notes: Chapter opener photo. The caption already explains it, so a short alt text and no long description is the expected outcome.

figures.caption: Figure 2.2
figures.x_axis: Number of Times Teenager is Reminded

reference.alt_text: Line graph of how often 40 teenagers must be reminded to do chores; frequency peaks at 3 reminders (14 parents).
reference.long_description: Line graph. The horizontal axis is Number of Times Teenager is Reminded, from 0 to 6; the vertical axis is Frequency, from 0 to 16. Points connected by line segments: 0 times, 2; 1 time, 5; 2 times, 8; 3 times, 14; 4 times, 7; 5 times, 4. The frequency rises to a peak at 3 reminders and then falls.

figures.notes: The x-axis runs to 6 but there is no point at 6.

reference.alt_text: Bar graph of U.S. TikTok users by age group; the share falls from 32.5% for ages 10–19 to 7.1% for ages 50 and over.
reference.long_description: Bar graph titled Proportion (%) of TikTok Users. The horizontal axis is Age Groups and the vertical axis is Proportion (%) of TikTok Users, from 0% to 35%. Ages 10–19: 32.5%. Ages 20–29: 29.5%. Ages 30–39: 16.4%. Ages 40–49: 13.9%. Ages 50+: 7.1%. Each older age group has a smaller share than the one before.

figures.caption: Figure 2.5
figures.values_source: Example 2.7 data list (pp. 87–88), binned at the boundaries given on p. 88; the bars are also labeled with these values

reference.alt_text: Histogram of the heights of 100 soccer players; the tallest bar, 0.40, is for 65.95 to 67.95 inches.
reference.long_description: Histogram of the heights, in inches, of 100 semiprofessional soccer players. The horizontal axis is Heights, with class boundaries every 2 inches from 59.95 to 75.95; the vertical axis is Relative Frequency, from 0 to 0.4. Each bar is labeled with its value: 59.95–61.95, 0.05; 61.95–63.95, 0.03; 63.95–65.95, 0.15; 65.95–67.95, 0.40; 67.95–69.95, 0.17; 69.95–71.95, 0.12; 71.95–73.95, 0.07; 73.95–75.95, 0.01. Most heights are between 63.95 and 71.95 inches, with a single peak at 65.95–67.95.

figures.notes: Values are printed on the bars, so they must match exactly. The x tick labels are rotated.

figures.caption: Figure 2.6

reference.alt_text: Histogram of books bought by 50 part-time students; 3 books is most common (16 students).
reference.long_description: Histogram of the number of books bought by 50 part-time college students. The horizontal axis is Number of Books, with bar boundaries at 0.5, 1.5, 2.5, 3.5, 4.5, 5.5 and 6.5; the vertical axis is Frequency, from 0 to 16. 1 book, 11 students; 2 books, 10; 3 books, 16; 4 books, 6; 5 books, 5; 6 books, 2. The distribution peaks at 3 books and tails off toward 6.

figures.notes: Values are not printed on the bars; read off the axis.

figures.caption: Figure 2.9
figures.title: Final Test Grade v Final Grade
figures.values_source: Tables 2.16 and 2.17 (p. 94), plotted at class midpoints, with the empty end classes the text describes for Figure 2.8

reference.alt_text: Two overlaid frequency polygons comparing calculus final test scores and final grades; both peak at 84.5.
reference.long_description: Two frequency polygons drawn on the same axes, titled Final Test Grade v Final Grade. The horizontal axis is Grades, at class midpoints from 44.5 to 104.5; the vertical axis is Frequency, from 0 to 50. Final test scores: 44.5, 0; 54.5, 5; 64.5, 10; 74.5, 30; 84.5, 40; 94.5, 15; 104.5, 0. Final grades: 44.5, 0; 54.5, 10; 64.5, 10; 74.5, 30; 84.5, 45; 94.5, 5; 104.5, 0. Both rise to a peak at 84.5. Final grades have more values at 54.5 and 84.5 and fewer at 94.5 than test scores.

figures.notes: Review is a correct outcome: The two series differ only by color and the crop has no legend, so the image alone cannot say which line is test scores and which is final grades. Two series, told apart only by color (dark and light blue), with no legend in the crop. Which line is which comes from the tables: light blue = final grades (10 at 54.5, 45 at 84.5).

figures.caption: Figure 2.10
figures.title: Annual CPI

reference.alt_text: Time series of the annual Consumer Price Index over 10 years, rising from 184.0 in year 1 to 229.6 in year 10.
reference.long_description: Time series graph titled Annual CPI. The horizontal axis is Year, 1 to 10; the vertical axis is Annual Consumer Price Index, from 180 to 240. Year 1, 184.0; year 2, 188.9; year 3, 195.3; year 4, 201.6; year 5, 207.3; year 6, 215.3; year 7, 214.5; year 8, 218.1; year 9, 224.9; year 10, 229.6. The index rises every year except for a small dip from year 6 to year 7.

figures.notes: Values in the figure must be read off the axis; the textbook values have up to 3 decimals.

figures.caption: Figure 2.11
figures.values_source: Data and five-number summary in the text (p. 107)

reference.alt_text: Box plot on a number line from 1 to 11.5: minimum 1, first quartile 2, median 7, third quartile 9, maximum 11.5.
reference.long_description: Box plot above a horizontal number line marked from 1 to 11.5. The left whisker runs from the minimum, 1, to the first quartile, 2. The box runs from 2 to the third quartile, 9, with the median at 7 shown as a dashed line. The right whisker runs from 9 to the maximum, 11.5. The left part of the box (2 to 7) is much wider than the right part (7 to 9).

figures.caption: Figure 2.14
figures.values_source: Example 2.24 solution, parts a and b (p. 109)

reference.alt_text: Two box plots of statistics test scores on one number line, day class above night class; the night class box is narrower and higher.
reference.long_description: Two box plots on one number line from 20 to 100. Upper plot (day class): minimum 32, first quartile 56, median 74.5, third quartile 82.5, maximum 99. Lower plot (night class): minimum 25.5, first quartile 78, median 81, third quartile 89, maximum 98. The day class has a much wider box, so the middle 50% of its scores are more spread out. The night class scores are concentrated higher, but it has a long left whisker down to 25.5.

figures.notes: Review is a correct outcome: The figure does not label which box plot is the day class and which the night class; that is only knowable from the text. The figure itself does not label which plot is day and which is night; the order (day on top) comes from matching the summaries. A good description should say the labels are not shown, or use the text.

figures.caption: Figure 2.16

reference.alt_text: Symmetrical histogram of values 4 to 10, peaking at 7; the mean, median and mode are all 7.
reference.long_description: Histogram of 16 values with one bar for each whole number from 4 to 10. Frequencies: 4, 1; 5, 1; 6, 3; 7, 6; 8, 3; 9, 1; 10, 1. The shape is symmetrical around 7, which is the single peak. The vertical axis has gridlines but no numbers or title.

figures.notes: No axis titles and no y-axis numbers: values can only be checked against the text. A description that gives exact counts read from the image is guessing.

figures.caption: Figure 2.19 Terry’s distribution has a right (positive) skew.
figures.title: Terry’s Letter Count

reference.alt_text: Dot plot of Terry's letter counts on a 1 to 10 scale, clustered at 1 to 4 with a peak at 3 and two high values, 7 and 9.
reference.long_description: Dot plot titled Terry’s Letter Count, on a number line from 1 to 10, with one X per value. 1: one X. 2: two. 3: four. 4: one. 7: one. 9: one. No values at 5, 6, 8 or 10. Most values sit at 1 to 4; the two values at 7 and 9 give the distribution a right (positive) skew.

figures.caption: Figure 2.25
figures.values_source: Example 2.33 data and solution (pp. 123–124); histogram counts computed from the data at the solution's interval endpoints

reference.alt_text: Box plot drawn above a histogram of 31 exam scores from 32.5 to 100.5; the highest bar is 86.9 to 100.5.
reference.long_description: A box plot and a histogram on the same horizontal axis, marked 32.5, 46.1, 59.7, 73.3, 73.5, 86.9 and 100.5, for 31 first-exam scores. Box plot: minimum 33, first quartile 61, median 73, third quartile 90, maximum 100. Histogram with five intervals of width 13.6: 32.5–46.1, 2 scores; 46.1–59.7, 5; 59.7–73.3, 9; 73.3–86.9, 4; 86.9–100.5, 11. The scores are skewed left: most are high, with a long tail of lower scores.

figures.notes: Review is a correct outcome: The drawn bar heights do not scale with the counts computed from the data, the y-axis has no numbers, and the 73.3 / 73.5 ticks are ambiguous; a verifier should see the readings disagree. Check: the drawn bar heights do not scale exactly with these counts, and the y-axis has no numbers. The axis shows both 73.3 and 73.5; the text gives median 73 and mean 73.5. Confirm what the dashed line and the 73.5 tick mark.

figures.caption: Figure 2.30

reference.alt_text: Empty graph axes for sketching a histogram: Frequency on the vertical axis, Number of Pairs of Shoes on the horizontal axis.
reference.long_description: Blank axes for students to draw their own histogram in the stats lab. The vertical axis is labeled Frequency and the horizontal axis Number of Pairs of Shoes. There are no scales, bars or data.

figures.notes: Review is a correct outcome: Blank axes with no data: a person should confirm that an empty-graph description is right (an auto-approved description is also fine if it invents nothing). Trap figure: there are no data. Any number or trend in the description is invented.

figures.caption: Figure 2.44

reference.alt_text: Box plots of foreign countries visited by 20-year-olds in China, Germany and the U.S., on a 0 to 11 scale.
reference.long_description: Three box plots on one number line from 0 to 11, showing how many foreign countries 20-year-olds had visited. China: only a line from 0 to 5 is drawn, with no box. Germany: whiskers from 0 to 11, box from about 4 to 8, with the median at the right edge of the box, about 8. United States: box from 0 to about 5 with the median at about 2, and a whisker out to 11. Germany has the highest median; the United States has the most values at the low end.

figures.notes: No numbers in the text; values are null. The numbers in the draft are read by eye from the figure. China is drawn without a box, which is an unusual case worth describing as drawn.

figures.caption: Figure 2.47

reference.alt_text: Box plots of buyers' ages for BMW 3, 5 and 7 series cars on a 25 to 80 scale; the 7 series has the oldest buyers.
reference.long_description: Three box plots on one number line from 25 to 80, showing the ages of 130 buyers each of new BMW 3, 5 and 7 series cars. 3 series: whiskers from about 23 to about 66, box from about 28 to 41, median about 33. 5 series: whiskers from about 32 to about 63, box from about 39 to 55, median about 41. 7 series: whiskers from about 36 to about 67, box from about 41 to 59, median about 46. All three are skewed right; median age rises from the 3 series to the 7 series.

figures.notes: No exact values in the text; values are null. The draft numbers are read by eye. The solutions (p. 176) give only estimates for the 5 series: second quarter about 3 years, third quarter about 14 years, IQR about 17 years.

figures.caption: Figure 2.58
figures.title: Births in Scotland

reference.alt_text: Time series of births in Scotland, 1855–1875: total births rise from 93,349 to 123,578, with male and female lines below.
reference.long_description: Time series graph titled Births in Scotland, with three lines for 1855 to 1875. The horizontal axis is Year; the vertical axis is Number of Births, from 40,000 to 130,000. Both sexes: 93,349 in 1855, rising to 123,711 in 1874 and 123,578 in 1875. Males: 47,804 in 1855 to 63,432 in 1875. Females: 45,545 in 1855 to 60,146 in 1875. All three rise over the period with small dips, for example in 1860 and 1869. Male births are slightly above female births every year. The full yearly values are in the data table.

figures.notes: Small text, 21 x-axis labels rotated, three series told apart by color and a legend at the bottom. Hardest chart in the set to read.

figures.caption: Figure 2.59
figures.values_source: Solution 75a (pp. 172–173); the measure is from Exercise 75 (p. 147, Table 2.62)

reference.alt_text: Bar graph of the percent of adults never married in 8 sampled states; Mississippi is highest at 34.0%, Washington DC lowest at 22.2%.
reference.long_description: Bar graph of the percent of adults who were never married, for a random sample of 8 states and Washington DC. The vertical axis is Percent (%), from 0 to 40. Arkansas 30.1; Washington DC 22.2; Idaho 26.5; Maryland 27.1; Michigan 30.9; Mississippi 34.0; Virginia 26.0; Wyoming 25.1. Values range from 22.2 to 34.0, mostly between 25 and 31.

figures.notes: The x labels are rotated and DC is written 'Wash DC'. The figure does not say what the percent measures (adults never married); that comes from Exercise 75.
